wwyd.objective: Ask about suicide directly and act the same day

beats.says: “Honestly, nothing matters anymore. Everyone would be fine without me.”

choices.text: “It sounds like things feel really heavy. Are you having thoughts of ending your life?”
choices.consequence: She pauses, then says yes, sometimes at night. You now know what you're dealing with.

choices.text: “Don't say that! Your family loves you.”
choices.consequence: She feels dismissed and says “forget it”. The risk is still there, and now it's hidden.

choices.text: “Let's focus on your studies first, then we'll talk feelings.”
choices.consequence: You get exam details, but you've skipped the most important question.

beats.says: “Sometimes I think about taking all my mother's sleeping pills.”
beats.context: She has access to the pills. No previous attempt.

choices.text: Ask about intent and timing, make a safety plan, and involve your supervisor today
choices.consequence: She agrees to her mother keeping the pills and to a follow-up tomorrow. Your supervisor reviews her the same day.

choices.text: Promise to keep it between the two of you so she trusts you
choices.consequence: You've made a promise you can't keep. If she's at risk, you must act, and she'll feel betrayed.

choices.text: Book her next weekly session as usual
choices.consequence: She's still at risk for 7 days with access to the means. Risk needs same-day action.

wwyd.objective: Spot mania and an antidepressant trigger

beats.says: “I haven't slept in 4 days and I've never felt better! I'm launching three companies.”

choices.text: Ask about sleep, spending, risky decisions and past depressions
choices.consequence: You learn she spent ₹2 lakh this week and had a long depression last year. Mania is likely.
You've reinforced the grandiosity and missed a probable manic episode.
Sleep matters, but this needs a psychiatric review, not a handout.

beats.says: “My GP gave me an antidepressant last month for low mood.”

choices.text: Flag it urgently to the psychiatrist: an antidepressant alone may have triggered mania
choices.consequence: The psychiatrist reviews her the same day and changes the plan.

choices.text: Tell her to stop the tablet today
choices.consequence: Medicine changes are the prescriber's job. Stopping suddenly can cause other problems.
It's documented, but a key safety issue wasn't escalated.

wwyd.objective: Respond to delusions without arguing or agreeing, then assess command voices

beats.says: “The voices say you're working with my neighbours. Are you recording me?”

choices.text: “I'm not recording you. It sounds frightening to feel watched. Can you tell me about the voices?”
choices.consequence: He relaxes slightly and describes two voices commenting on him.

choices.text: “There are no voices. That's just your illness talking.”
choices.consequence: Arguing with a delusion breaks trust. He stops talking.

choices.text: “Okay, yes, let's say the neighbours are involved.”
choices.consequence: Agreeing with the delusion reinforces it and isn't honest.

beats.says: “The voices tell me to hurt the neighbour's dog.”

choices.text: Ask if he plans to act, whether he's acted before, and inform the psychiatrist today
choices.consequence: Command hallucinations with possible action need urgent review. The team acts in time.

choices.text: Reassure him that voices can't make him do anything
choices.consequence: Kind, but you haven't assessed the risk.

choices.text: Change the topic to keep him calm
choices.consequence: You've avoided a risk you were told about.

sct.vignette: A 24-year-old woman comes in with 2 months of poor sleep, low energy, and tearfulness. She says she's 'just stressed' about work.
sct.new_information: Her appetite has increased and she has gained 4 kg. She sleeps 12+ hours on weekends.

sct.vignette: A 30-year-old man reports palpitations, sweating, and fear of dying that started 3 months ago on the metro. Cardiac workup was normal.
sct.new_information: He now avoids buses and crowds, and has stopped going to the gym because 'the heart thing' might happen there.

sct.vignette: A 19-year-old student has intrusive blasphemous thoughts and washes his hands 30 times a day. He is ashamed and thinks he's 'possessed'.
sct.new_information: He has missed 11 days of college this semester because of the washing rituals.

sct.vignette: A 45-year-old businessman is brought by his wife for 'drinking too much'. He denies it and says business stress is the issue.
sct.new_information: He drives home from work after drinking most evenings.

sct.vignette: A 26-year-old woman, 6 months postpartum, says she's 'not a good mother' and cries daily. Her mother-in-law does most of the childcare.
sct.new_information: She has had thoughts of 'the baby would be better off without me': passive, no plan.

sct.vignette: A 60-year-old retired teacher, 8 months after his wife's death, talks to her chair and sorts her clothes one drawer a week.
sct.new_information: He laughs with his grandchildren, eats well, and sleeps except on anniversaries.

ethics.vignette: A 41-year-old man with recurrent major depressive disorder has an advance directive on file refusing ECT. He arrives in a severe catatonic state, can't give consent, and his family demands 'the shock treatment' because it worked before. The treating psychiatrist asks your opinion on the next legal step.

options.label: Proceed with ECT: the family's consent overrides a document.
options.consequence: The advance directive is a legal instrument under MHA 2017, not a family preference. Treating against it without invoking Section 5(4) is a breach with professional consequences. The nominated representative's consent is the right pathway, but they consent within the directive's limits, not over it.

options.label: Honour the advance directive: ECT is barred by MHA 2017 Section 5.
options.consequence: Correct. An advance directive refusing a treatment binds the treating team unless one of the narrow Section 5(4) exceptions applies (a high risk of death or irreversible harm and no other equally effective option). You would first treat the catatonia with benzodiazepines and pursue consent from the nominated representative, not default to ECT.

options.label: Ignore both and transfer: a catatonic patient is someone else's problem.
options.consequence: Transfer is legitimate only if the receiving facility is genuinely better placed. Using it to dodge a hard legal decision is abandonment. You stay clinically responsible until the handover is complete.

ethics.law: MHA 2017 Section 5: advance directives bind the treating team; exceptions are narrow and must be invoked, not assumed.

ethics.vignette: A 14-year-old tells you that a distant relative has been touching her on school-pickup days and 'says it's our secret'. She begs you not to tell her parents. POCSO is unambiguous about your duty. Which action comes first?

options.label: Promise to keep the secret to preserve the therapeutic alliance.
options.consequence: A promise you can't keep. POCSO removes the discretion, and a false promise teaches her that adults lie about safety. Alliance built on 'I can't keep this secret' is harder but real.

options.label: Call the parents first so they can handle it 'within the family'.
options.consequence: The abuser is a relative: telling the family first can tip them off and expose her to more harm before authorities are involved. Mandatory reporting goes to the designated channels; the family is informed as part of that process, not before it.

options.label: Inform the mandated authorities (police/Childline): the secrecy ends with you.
options.consequence: Correct. POCSO imposes a mandatory reporting duty; it also protects her from the relative continuing to groom. You don't require parental consent to report, and you're honest with her that you can't keep this secret because the law and her safety require otherwise. Confidentiality has limits you state up front.

ethics.law: POCSO 2012: mandatory reporting to police/Childline; failure is itself an offence. Confidentiality never covers child sexual abuse.

ethics.vignette: A client keeps asking you, a counselling psychologist, whether their antidepressant dose is 'right'. You've noticed they're oversedated in sessions. What's within your scope?

options.label: Advise them to halve the dose. You can 'see' it's too much.
options.consequence: Dose adjustment is a medical act. Advising it steps over the RCI scope line and, if something goes wrong, lands on you. You can describe what you observe; you can't prescribe the fix.

options.label: Note the observation, encourage adherence, and refer medication adjustment to the prescriber.
options.consequence: Correct. Sedation is a medication effect worth flagging, but titration is outside your scope. You document the observation and coordinate with the prescriber (with consent). This is the RCI boundary working as intended.

options.label: Stop raising it. It's not your place to notice medication at all.
options.consequence: You're allowed to observe and coordinate: the boundary is about adjusting, not noticing. Failing to flag an observation that matters is a duty-of-care miss, not professional restraint.

ethics.law: RCI scope of practice: counselling psychologists assess and support; prescribing and dose adjustment sit with medical practitioners.

landmark.title: Phineas Gage
landmark.story: In 1848, a railway foreman survived an iron rod through his frontal lobes. His friends said 'Gage was no longer Gage': the polite, reliable man became impulsive and profane.
landmark.believedThen: That personality lived in a single 'seat', and that the accident proved it was the front of the brain.
landmark.understandNow: The frontal lobes modulate behaviour, but personality is distributed. Gage is the origin story of 'executive function', and later accounts note his social recovery was better than the myth claimed.

quiz.question: What is Gage's lasting lesson?
options: The frontal lobes modulate impulse and social behaviour
quiz.rationale: Gage demonstrated that frontal damage changes social-emotional regulation: the founding case of executive function.

quiz.question: Why is the 'Gage was no longer Gage' account now qualified?
options: It was invented by the press
Later evidence shows significant social recovery, complicating the myth
quiz.rationale: Modern re-analysis suggests his functioning recovered more than the legend, teaching students to read famous cases critically.

quiz.question: What domain does Gage belong to?
quiz.rationale: Gage is a neuropsychology landmark: brain-behaviour mapping.

tags.objective: Link frontal lobe damage to changes in behaviour

landmark.title: H.M. (Henry Molaison)
landmark.story: To stop severe epilepsy, Molaison had both medial temporal lobes removed in 1953. The epilepsy improved. He could no longer form new memories: his life froze at the operation.
landmark.believedThen: Memory was a single faculty; the brain didn't 'store' experiences in a way an operation could destroy.
landmark.understandNow: H.M. revealed the distinction between declarative memory (what, gone for him) and procedural memory (how, intact). He could learn a mirror-tracing task and deny ever having seen it. That split is still the backbone of memory science.

quiz.question: H.M. taught us that memory is:
options: Divided into declarative and procedural systems
quiz.rationale: H.M.'s intact procedural learning alongside lost declarative memory proved memory is multiple systems.

quiz.question: Which task could H.M. learn despite his amnesia?
quiz.rationale: Procedural (skill) memory survived; declarative did not: mirror-tracing is a skill.

tags.objective: Explain the split between declarative and procedural memory

osce.title: Focused risk assessment
osce.task: Take a focused risk assessment of a 26-year-old woman who has been feeling 'very low' since a breakup.

checklist.item: Asked about suicidal ideation in clear language
Made a clear safety plan / referral

osce.role_brief: You are Ananya, 26, a bank clerk in Pune. Your boyfriend of four years ended things six weeks ago. You sleep badly and cry at work. If asked clearly, you say you have thought 'it would be easier not to wake up' most nights, and last week you looked at your mother's sleeping tablets but did not take any. You have no plan for tonight. Your younger sister matters a great deal to you. You drink 'a few' beers at weekends. Answer honestly when asked directly; volunteer nothing about the tablets.
model_points: Asks about suicide in plain words: 'Have you had thoughts of ending your life?'
Moves from thoughts to plan, means (the tablets), intent and timing, without flinching
Asks about past attempts, alcohol and who knows
Draws out the sister as a reason for living and uses it in the plan
Agrees a written safety plan: the tablets handed to her mother, a crisis number, a review within days

tags.objective: Run a structured suicide risk assessment and safety plan

osce.title: Explain an SSRI to a reluctant patient
osce.task: Explain what an SSRI is, what to expect, and address a 40-year-old man's fears that 'antidepressants are addictive'.

checklist.item: Discussed common side effects + what to do

osce.role_brief: You are Mr Sharma, 40, a transport supervisor. Your doctor wants you to start an antidepressant. Your cousin 'got hooked' on sleeping pills, and you think these are the same. You also worry about losing your sex drive. You will agree to a trial only if your fears are answered without lecturing.
model_points: Explains the medicine in plain words: it helps the brain's mood signalling settle over weeks
Sets the timeline: side effects may come first, benefit usually builds over 2 to 6 weeks
Separates antidepressants from sleeping pills: no craving or need for higher doses, but stopping suddenly can cause unpleasant discontinuation symptoms
Names common side effects, including sexual ones, and what to do about them
Invites his questions and lets him decide

tags.objective: Explain an SSRI and answer the addiction fear honestly

formulation.title: Ravi: 'the heaviness' (somatic depression)
formulation.prompt: Sort the factors into the 5P grid. Leave distractors out.

factors.text: Body ache, heaviness, poor sleep, 6kg weight loss
Promotion added night shifts 8 months ago
Father had a 'nervous breakdown' in his 40s
Avoids talking about feelings; keeps working while exhausted
Supportive wife who 'keeps asking'
GP visits for 'gas' and 'weakness' without improvement
Core belief: 'I am failing my family'
The weather is unusually hot this summer
Employee has a steady job and a roof
Two-year help-seeking delay before any mental-health contact

formulation.modelNarrative: Ravi presents with somatic depression: 8 months of body ache, broken sleep and weight loss following a promotion that added night shifts (precipitant). A family history of paternal 'nervous breakdown' and a core belief of failing his family (predisposing) shape his coping: he avoids disclosing distress and keeps working through exhaustion (perpetuating), and a two-year help-seeking delay reinforced it. Protective factors include a supportive wife and stable employment. The formulation explains why he presents somatically: the heaviness is the only acceptable language his belief system permits for distress.
formulation.hint: Somatic depression in a man who won't talk about feelings

tags.objective: Link a somatic presentation of depression to its 5 Ps
tags.diagnosis: Moderate depressive episode with somatic presentation

formulation.title: Meera: the exam that never ends (panic disorder)
formulation.prompt: Sort the factors into the 5P grid. Leave distractors out.
formulation.hint: Panic attacks before NEET, a heart she is sure is failing

factors.text: Sudden attacks of racing heart, breathlessness and fear of dying, 3 to 4 times a week
Now avoids the coaching centre and travels only with her mother
First attack in the exam hall, two months before her second NEET attempt
Mother has 'BP and tension' and checks her own pulse often
Anxious, perfectionistic temperament since childhood
Three ECGs and an echo, all normal; each one calms her for a day only
Carries a water bottle and sits near doors 'just in case' (safety behaviours)
Reads about heart attacks in young women late at night
Close friend who has offered to sit with her in class
Bright, motivated, and asked for help herself
Her blood group is B positive
The family recently bought a new scooter

formulation.modelNarrative: Meera, 19, presents with panic disorder with growing agoraphobic avoidance: frequent surges of palpitations, breathlessness and fear of dying, and she now avoids the coaching centre. An anxious, perfectionistic temperament and a mother who models health vigilance (predisposing) set the stage; the first attack came in the exam hall during a high-stakes repeat attempt (precipitating). The cycle is kept going by repeated reassurance-seeking through normal cardiac tests, safety behaviours that stop her learning the attacks are harmless, and night-time symptom searching (perpetuating). Her own help-seeking, intelligence and a supportive friend are strengths to build exposure work on (protective).

tags.objective: Show how safety behaviours and reassurance keep panic going
tags.diagnosis: Panic disorder with early agoraphobic avoidance
